blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 19 (Nuclear and Particle Physics), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe briefly how the nucleus and its constituents were discovered. Explain the nuclide symbol ᴬ_Z X and give the sizes of the nucleus and the atom. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Discovery:
• Ernest Rutherford's α-particle scattering experiments (1911) showed a dense, positively charged central part, the nucleus, of very small size, surrounded by electrons. Most of the atom is empty and its mass is concentrated in the nucleus.
• In 1920 Rutherford suggested that the positive charge is due to protons inside the nucleus and predicted a particle with no charge.
• James Chadwick discovered this particle, the neutron, in 1932.

Nuclide symbol ᴬ_Z X:
• X is the chemical symbol of the element.
• Z is the atomic or charge number: the number of protons.
• A is the mass number: the total number of nucleons (protons and neutrons).
• Number of neutrons N = A − Z.
Examples: ¹₁H, ¹²₆C, ²³⁵₉₂U.

Size: The nucleus is very dense, with a radius of the order 10⁻¹⁴ m; the cloud of electrons gives the atom a radius of the order 10⁻¹⁰ m.

book_ref.quote: In 1920, Rutherford further suggested the positive charge due to protons inside the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 2 For the nuclides ¹³¹₅₃I and ⁵⁹₂₆Fe find (i) the number of protons, (ii) the number of neutrons and (iii) the number of nucleons in each. Also find how many times the atomic radius (10⁻¹⁰ m) is larger than the nuclear radius (10⁻¹⁴ m). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Protons = Z, nucleons = A, neutrons = A − Z; the size ratio is a simple division.

book_ref.quote: Thus, we write the elements of hydrogen, carbon and uranium as

blocks.final_answer: I-131: 53 p, 78 n, 131 nucleons; Fe-59: 26 p, 33 n, 59 nucleons; atom about 10⁴ times larger

blocks.prompt: 3 Define mass defect and binding energy. Write the equation for the mass defect of a nucleus ᴬ_Z X and show how its binding energy is found. Also define binding energy per nucleon and the atomic mass unit. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Mass defect: Experiments show that the mass of a nucleus is always less than the total mass of the protons and neutrons making it up. The lost (missing) mass is the mass defect Δm. A nucleus ᴬ_Z X has Z protons and (A − Z) neutrons, so
Δm = [Zmₚ + (A − Z)mₙ] − m_nucleus ... (19.1)
where mₚ is the mass of a proton, mₙ of a neutron and m_nucleus of the whole nucleus.

Binding energy: The missing mass is converted into energy used in the formation of the nucleus. By Einstein's mass-energy relation
ΔE = (Δm)c² ... (19.2)
This energy is the binding energy (B.E): the work done on the nucleus to break it into its constituent neutrons and protons. Like absolute gravitational potential (zero at infinity), it is taken as negative for a bound system.

Binding energy per nucleon: B.E/A, the average energy needed to separate a nucleus into its individual nucleons; it is a better measure of stability.

Atomic mass unit: 1 u is one-twelfth of the mass of an atom of carbon-12.
1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg

book_ref.quote: The results of experiments on the masses of different nuclei show

blocks.prompt: 4 The mass of a tritium nucleus ³₁H is 5.007357 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Find its mass defect, binding energy in MeV and binding energy per nucleon. (mₚ = 1.672623 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, mₙ = 1.674929 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Tritium has 1 proton and 2 neutrons; find Δm from Eq. 19.1, then B.E = Δmc², change to eV and divide by A = 3.

book_ref.quote: Find the mass defect and binding energy of the helium nucleus given that

blocks.final_answer: Δm = 1.5124 × 10⁻²⁹ kg; B.E = 8.51 MeV; 2.84 MeV per nucleon

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe the graph of binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number. What does it tell about the stability of nuclei, and how does it explain the release of energy in fission and fusion? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The graph (Fig. 19.1) plots binding energy per nucleon against nucleon number A. The position of a nucleus on it tells how stable the nucleus is and whether energy can be obtained from it by fission or by fusion.

Features of the curve:
• The hydrogen nucleus (one proton) has zero binding energy.
• The step from hydrogen to helium is large, suggesting a large energy release when hydrogen is converted to helium.
• The curve reaches a maximum of about 8.7 MeV per nucleon for iron-56 (⁵⁶₂₆Fe), the most stable nuclide; the most stable nuclei lie between A = 50 and 80.
• After that, binding energy per nucleon decreases steadily to the end of the curve.
So binding energy per nucleon is less for very light and very heavy nuclei.

Fission: If a heavy nucleus splits into two middle nuclei, the products are more tightly bound (more stable), and energy is released. Mankind already obtains huge power from this.

Fusion: If a pair of light nuclei combine into one nucleus, the nucleons become more tightly bound; e.g. deuterium and tritium fusing to helium release huge energy. It needs an extremely high temperature, as in the Sun and stars.

Rule: energy is obtained from any nuclear reaction in which the binding energy per nucleon of the products increases.

book_ref.quote: The position of a nucleus on this curve gives information about the stability of the nucleus

blocks.prompt: 6 Using the chapter's table of masses (proton 1.007276 u, neutron 1.008665 u, electron 0.00055 u, atomic mass of ⁷₃Li 7.016004 u), find the binding energy of the ⁷₃Li nucleus in MeV and its binding energy per nucleon. (1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Remove the 3 electrons from the atomic mass to get the nuclear mass, then use Eq. 19.1 with 3 protons and 4 neutrons, and Eq. 19.2.

book_ref.quote: For your information: Some Atomic Masses

blocks.final_answer: B.E of ⁷₃Li ≈ 39.3 MeV; about 5.62 MeV per nucleon

blocks.prompt: 7 What is nuclear fission? Describe the discovery of fission of uranium-235, write its equation, and use the binding energy curve to estimate the energy released per fission. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: A reaction in which a heavy nucleus like uranium splits into two nuclei of roughly equal size, with the emission of energy, is called fission.

Discovery: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann (Germany) found that slow neutrons bombarding ²³⁵₉₂U give ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba, ⁹²₃₆Kr and on average three neutrons. It differed from other nuclear reactions in two ways: (1) two nuclei of almost equal size are obtained; (2) a very large amount of energy is given out.

Equation:
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + 3¹₀n + Q ... (19.3)
The sums of mass numbers (236) and of charge numbers (92) are the same on both sides. Comparing total energies gives about 200 MeV per fission.

Energy from the curve: Binding energy per nucleon is greatest for middle elements and less for very heavy ones. For uranium it is about 7.6 MeV, for barium and krypton about 8.5 MeV. So energy per nucleon = 8.5 − 7.6 = 0.9 MeV, and for 235 nucleons:
E = 235 × 0.9 = 211.5 MeV ≈ 200 MeV

Other fragments: fission does not always give Ba and Kr, e.g.
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹³²₅₀Sn + ¹⁰¹₄₂Mo + 3¹₀n + Q ... (19.4)
²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁰₅₄Xe + ⁹⁴₃₈Sr + 2¹₀n + Q ... (19.5)
All fission fragments are radioactive. Fission occurs very easily with slow neutrons in uranium-235 and plutonium-239.

book_ref.quote: Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann of Germany

blocks.prompt: 8 Each fission of uranium-235 releases about 200 MeV. Find the total energy released when 1.0 g of uranium-235 undergoes complete fission. (Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, molar mass of uranium-235 = 235 g mol⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the number of nuclei in 1 g, change 200 MeV into joules, and multiply.

book_ref.quote: By comparing the total energy on the left side of the equation

steps: Number of nuclei N = (1.0 g × 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹)/235 g mol⁻¹ = 2.56 × 10²¹
blocks.final_answer: E ≈ 8.2 × 10¹⁰ J from 1.0 g of uranium-235

blocks.prompt: 9 What is a fission chain reaction? Explain critical mass and critical volume, and describe what happens when the mass of uranium is less than, equal to or much greater than the critical mass. How is the chain reaction controlled? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Chain reaction: A uranium-235 nucleus absorbs a neutron, splits into two nuclei of almost equal mass and emits two or three neutrons. If these neutrons produce fission in more uranium atoms, the reaction maintains itself; this is a fission chain reaction (Fig. 19.3). Uncontrolled, it proceeds rapidly and in an extremely small time gives a large amount of energy with a huge explosion.

Role of size (Fig. 19.4):
(a) In a thin sheet of fissile material the neutrons scatter into the air; no chain reaction.
(b) Under more favourable conditions, some neutrons cause only one more fission; still no chain reaction.
(c) In a sufficiently big spherical lump most neutrons are absorbed before they escape, producing a chain reaction.

Critical mass: the mass of uranium in which one neutron, out of all those produced in one fission, produces further fission. Its volume is the critical volume or size.
• Mass less than critical: the chain reaction does not proceed.
• Mass equal to critical: it proceeds at its initial speed; a steady source of energy, used in an atomic reactor.
• Mass much greater than critical: it proceeds rapidly with a huge explosion; the atom bomb works on this.

Control: In a reactor the reaction is controlled by rods, usually of cadmium, which absorb many neutrons without becoming unstable or radioactive. Inserting them cuts down the neutrons available for fission, so that on the average only one neutron from each fission causes another fission and energy is released at a steady rate.

book_ref.quote: By properly using these neutrons, fission reaction can be produced in more uranium atoms

blocks.prompt: 10 A reactor runs on a controlled chain reaction and produces thermal power of 500 MW. If each fission releases 200 MeV, find (i) the number of fissions per second and (ii) the mass of uranium-235 used per day. (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, molar mass 235 g mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Power ÷ energy per fission gives fissions per second; multiply by seconds in a day and convert nuclei to grams.

book_ref.quote: In this way, the fission reaction is controlled.

steps: Fissions per second = 500 × 10⁶ W / 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J = 1.5625 × 10¹⁹ s⁻¹ ≈ 1.56 × 10¹⁹ s⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: (i) 1.56 × 10¹⁹ fissions per second; (ii) about 527 g of uranium-235 per day

blocks.prompt: 11 Describe a nuclear power reactor. Explain the function of its core, moderator, control rods and heat exchanger, and describe how electricity is produced and how nuclear waste is stored. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Principle: In a nuclear power station the reactor plays the part of the furnace of a thermal power station. Fission (about 200 MeV per nucleus) gives kinetic energy to the fission fragments; their collisions turn it into heat. The heat makes steam, the steam turns the turbine and the turbine turns the generator (Fig. 19.5).

1. Core: the most vital part, where fuel is kept in cylindrical tubes. Fuel: uranium enriched to 2.4-3.0% uranium-235 (natural uranium has only 0.7%); nowadays also plutonium-239 and uranium-233.

2. Moderator: the fuel rods are placed in a substance of small atomic weight such as water or heavy water (made of ²₁H). Fission neutrons are very fast and unsuitable for fission; the moderator slows them down because slow neutrons are more useful.

3. Control rods: rods of cadmium or boron, which absorb slow (thermal) neutrons strongly, are moved in or out of the core so that, of all neutrons produced, only one causes further fission. In an emergency or for repair the rods fall back into the reactor and stop the chain reaction.

4. Heat exchanger: the core reaches about 500 °C. Water, heavy water or another liquid under high pressure carries the heat to the heat exchanger, where it produces high temperature steam from ordinary water. Steam leaving the turbine (about 300 °C) is cooled back to water using river or sea water.

Waste: fuel lasts a few months; the used fuel stays intensely radioactive with half-lives of many thousand years. It must not reach oceans, soil, air or drinking water; the best place found is the bottom of old, very dry salt mines thousands of metres below the surface.

book_ref.quote: A reactor usually has four important parts. These are:

blocks.prompt: 12 A reactor core contains 2.0 kg of uranium-235. If the reactor's thermal power is 300 MW and each fission releases 200 MeV, how many days would it take to use up 10% of this uranium-235? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, molar mass 235 g mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the number of nuclei in 10% of the fuel, the fissions per second, and divide.

book_ref.quote: When fission takes place in the atom of uranium or any other heavy atom

blocks.final_answer: About 5.5 × 10⁴ s, i.e. about 0.63 day (15 hours)

blocks.prompt: 13 What is nuclear fusion? Explain why energy is released in fusion and why fusion is difficult to produce. Write fusion reactions of deuterium and tritium and describe the methods used to produce fusion. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: A nuclear reaction in which two light nuclei merge to form a heavier nucleus is called fusion.

Why energy is released: The binding energy curve shows that binding energy per nucleon increases up to A = 50. When two light nuclei merge into a nucleus with A less than 50, some mass is lost and its equivalent energy is given out. Fusion gives more energy per nucleon than fission.

Why it is difficult: Both nuclei are positively charged. To bring them very close, work must be done against their electrostatic repulsion, so a very large amount of energy is needed to start fusion.

Reactions:
²₁H + ²₁H → ³₁H + ¹₁H + 4.0 MeV ... (19.6)
²₁H + ²₁H → ³₂He + ¹₀n + 3.3 MeV ... (19.7)
Each gives about 1.0 MeV per nucleon. Deuterium and tritium (the fusion fuels) give
²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV ... (19.8)

Methods:
1. Accelerator: the nuclei are given very large velocities and collided (Fig. 19.6); used in research but not for large-scale continuous energy.
2. High temperature: the speed of atoms increases with temperature; at about 10 million °C light nuclei get the required speed. Such a reaction is a thermonuclear reaction. This temperature is reached for a very short time in an atom bomb explosion, which triggers the hydrogen bomb.

Fusion has not yet been controlled like fission, so it is not used to make electricity; it takes place in the core of stars including the Sun.

book_ref.quote: The curve of the graph in Fig. 19.1 also shows that the binding energy per nucleon increases up to A = 50.

blocks.prompt: 14 In the fusion ²₁H + ³₁H → ⁴₂He + ¹₀n + 17.6 MeV, find (i) the energy released in joules, (ii) the mass converted into energy and (iii) the energy per nucleon, and compare it with the 0.9 MeV per nucleon of fission. (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Convert MeV to J, use Δm = E/c², and divide 17.6 MeV by the 5 nucleons taking part.

book_ref.quote: During a fusion reaction some mass is lost and its equivalent energy is given out.

steps: Nucleons taking part = 2 + 3 = 5; energy per nucleon = 17.6/5 = 3.52 MeV
blocks.final_answer: (i) 2.82 × 10⁻¹² J; (ii) 3.13 × 10⁻²⁹ kg; (iii) 3.52 MeV per nucleon, about 3.9 times that of fission

blocks.prompt: 15 Define activity and its SI unit. Show that the number of atoms decaying in a short interval is ΔN = −λNΔt, explain the meaning of the decay constant, and obtain the relation between activity and decay constant. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Random decay: When an α- or β-particle is emitted, the element changes into another element. Decay is random: we cannot predict when a particular atom will decay, but a very large sample follows a consistent pattern (Fig. 19.7).

Activity: the number of particles a radioactive substance emits per second. SI unit: becquerel, 1 Bq = 1 decay per second. The count rate of a detector (counts per second) is directly proportional to the activity.

Decay law: If N radioactive atoms are present at a time, the number ΔN decaying in a short interval Δt is proportional to Δt and to N. Since N decreases,
ΔN ∝ −NΔt
ΔN = −λNΔt ... (19.9)
λ is the constant of proportionality, the decay constant.

Meaning of λ: λ = −(ΔN/N)/Δt is the fraction of the atoms decaying per unit time; its unit is s⁻¹. A large λ means more atoms decay in a given interval. The minus sign shows the decrease of N.

Activity and λ: dividing Eq. 19.9 by Δt,
ΔN/Δt = −λN
The activity is the (positive) number of decays per second, so
A = −ΔN/Δt = λN ... (19.10)
Thus activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei.

book_ref.quote: We can represent these results with an equation.

blocks.prompt: 16 A sample of sodium-24 (half-life 15 hours, molar mass 24 g mol⁻¹) has a mass of 2.0 μg. Find (i) the number of nuclei, (ii) the decay constant and (iii) the activity of the sample. (Avogadro's number 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Number of nuclei from mass and molar mass; λ = 0.693/T½ with T½ in seconds; then A = λN.

book_ref.quote: Its sample of mass 5.1 μg is found to have an activity

blocks.prompt: 17 Define half-life. Show that after n half-lives the number of undecayed atoms is (1/2)ⁿN₀ and the number decayed is N₀(1 − 1/2ⁿ). What two conclusions follow about radioactive decay? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The time taken for the activity of a sample to decrease to half of any starting value is the half-life T½. Every element has its own half-life, e.g. uranium-238 4.5 × 10⁹ years, radium-226 1620 years, radon 3.8 days, uranium-239 23.5 minutes.

Atoms left: Let N₀ atoms be present at the start (decay curve, Fig. 19.7).
After one half-life: N₀/2 left
After two half-lives: ½ × N₀/2 = (1/2)²N₀ left
After three half-lives: ½ × (1/2)²N₀ = (1/2)³N₀ left
After n half-lives: N = (1/2)ⁿN₀

Atoms decayed:
After first half-life = N₀ − N₀/2 = N₀/2
After second half-life = N₀ − N₀/4 = 3N₀/4
After third half-life = N₀ − N₀/8 = 7N₀/8
After n half-lives: decayed = N₀(1 − 1/2ⁿ) ... (19.11)

Conclusions:
1. No radioactive element can decay completely: in each half-life only half of the remaining nuclei decay, so an infinite time would be needed for all atoms to decay.
2. The number of atoms decaying in a period is proportional to the number present at the beginning of that period: a large number gives many decays, a small number few.

book_ref.quote: After a period of one half-life N₀ / 2 number of atoms of this radioactive element are left behind.

blocks.prompt: 18 Iodine-131 has a half-life of 8 days. A sample initially contains 4800 atoms of iodine-131. Find (i) the number of atoms left and (ii) the number decayed after 32 days, and (iii) the percentage left. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Count the half-lives in 32 days, then use N = (1/2)ⁿN₀ and decayed = N₀(1 − 1/2ⁿ).

book_ref.quote: If there are 1000 atoms of polonium initially present in a sample

steps: Number of half-lives n = 32 days / 8 days = 4

blocks.prompt: 19 Write the exponential law of radioactive decay. Using it, obtain the relation between half-life and decay constant, and explain what the decay curve shows. Also explain how artificial radioactive elements are made. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Exponential law: The decay of a radioactive element can be described by its half-life or its decay constant λ. With calculus, the number of undecayed nuclei N after time t is
N = N₀e^(−λt) ... (19.12)
where N₀ is the initial number of nuclides.

Half-life: When N reduces to N₀/2, t = T½:
N₀/2 = N₀e^(−λT½)
e^(λT½) = 2
λT½ = ln 2 = 0.693
T½ = 0.693/λ ... (19.13)
So if λ is known, the half-life can be found, and vice versa; a large λ means a short half-life.

Decay curve: A graph of the number of atoms present against time (Fig. 19.7) starts at N₀ and falls to N₀/2, N₀/4, N₀/8, … after each half-life. It never reaches zero. Every radioactive element follows this curve, but each has a different half-life.

Artificial radioactive elements: Any stable element can be made radioactive by bombarding it with very high energy particles. The bombardment excites the nuclei, which become unstable and radioactive; these are artificial radioactive elements.

book_ref.quote: When N reduces to N₀/2, t is known as half-life

blocks.explanation: Get λ from T½ = 0.693/λ, then put λt into the exponential.

book_ref.quote: The solution of Eq. 19.12 gives,

blocks.final_answer: (i) λ = 3.21 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹; (ii) 0.0625 (1/16) of the sample is left; (iii) confirmed

blocks.prompt: 21 What are radioactive tracers? Explain the tracer technique and describe the uses of radioisotopes in medical diagnosis and treatment and in agriculture. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Tracer: A radioactive isotope behaves in just the same way as the normal isotope inside a living organism, but its location and concentration are found easily by measuring its radiation. So it acts as an indicator or tracer to follow a chemical or biological process.

Technique: radioactive atoms are substituted for stable atoms of the same kind in a substance, and the 'tagged' atoms are followed with a radiation detector. Radioisotopes are made easily by bombardment with neutrons and other particles and are inexpensive.

Medical diagnosis:
• Tracers show digestion and how chemicals move in the body. Radio-iodine is absorbed mostly by the thyroid gland, phosphorus by bones and cobalt by the liver.
• A small, low-activity dose shows whether the thyroid works properly; a diseased or hyperactive gland absorbs more than twice the normal amount.
• Sodium-24 is used to study blood circulation. Table 19.1 lists more, e.g. sodium-24 (15 hours) for plasma volume, iron-59 (45 days) for iron in plasma, technetium-99m (6 hours) for thyroid uptake scans.

Treatment:
• Rapidly multiplying cancer cells absorb more radiation and are destroyed more easily than normal cells. Iodine-131 is used against thyroid cancer.
• Radioisotope capsules called 'seeds' are implanted in malignant tissue for local treatment; phosphorus-32 or strontium-90 may be used for skin cancer, with the dose carefully controlled to protect healthy tissue.

Agriculture and research: a little radioisotope mixed with fertilizer shows how much fertilizer a plant takes up; radiation-induced mutations gave improved rice, chickpea, wheat and cotton. In chemistry and biology, radioisotopes show how complex reactions proceed.

book_ref.quote: A radioactive isotope behaves in just the same way as the normal isotope inside a living organism.

blocks.prompt: 22 A patient is given a dose of iodine-131 (half-life 8 days) with an activity of 4.0 × 10⁸ Bq. Find (i) the activity after 24 days, (ii) the decay constant of iodine-131 and (iii) the number of iodine-131 nuclei in the original dose. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Activity halves every half-life; λ = 0.693/T½ in s⁻¹; N = A/λ.

book_ref.quote: For radioactive Iodine-131 is also used to combat cancer of the thyroid gland.

blocks.prompt: 23 What is annihilation of matter? Explain the annihilation of an electron-positron pair and why two photons are produced. Describe how high energy collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider are used in particle research. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Annihilation: an event that takes place whenever a particle and its antiparticle come close to each other. Both disappear and their mass is converted into energy by Einstein's relation.

Electron-positron pair: an electron and a positron each of mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg annihilate. The energy produced is
E = 2mc²
which works out to about 1.02 MeV (Example 19.4).
Two photons: the pair at rest has zero total momentum. So two γ-ray photons, each of 0.51 MeV, are emitted travelling in opposite directions, keeping the total momentum zero (conservation of momentum).

High energy collisions: elementary particle research needs very high energies. Instead of collisions at rest-mass energies, particles are accelerated to nearly the speed of light and then collided. At CERN's Large Hadron Collider protons are collided with protons, and heavy nuclei with each other, at energies of the order of TeV, creating conditions similar to the early universe (a 7 TeV proton-proton collision in CMS produced more than 100 charged particles).

Discoveries: the electro-weak force mediating W⁺, W⁻ and Z bosons were predicted by Prof. Abdus Salam; the most significant discovery at the LHC is the Higgs boson, in July 2012.

book_ref.quote: In elementary particles research, very high energies are required for investigations.

blocks.prompt: 24 A proton (mass 1.672623 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) and an antiproton of the same mass annihilate at rest, producing two γ-ray photons. Find (i) the total energy released in joules, (ii) the energy of each photon in MeV and (iii) how many times this is the energy of each photon from electron-positron annihilation (0.51 MeV). (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use E = 2mc² as in Example 19.4, share it equally between the two photons, then compare.

book_ref.quote: Using Einstein mass-energy relation E = 2mc²

blocks.final_answer: (i) 3.01 × 10⁻¹⁰ J; (ii) about 941 MeV per photon; (iii) about 1.8 × 10³ times
